newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New crew set to blast off as woes mount on Mir.
newsitem.headline: New crew set to blast off as woes mount on Mir.

text.p: Two new cosmonauts were due to blast off on Tuesday to relieve the beleaguered crew of Mir, who continued to face problems with the oxygen-generating system on the ailing space station.

Veteran commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov, 43, depart from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan at 1536 GMT on Tuesday knowing the repairs they attempt will determine the future of the 11-year-old station.

Their first major repair will be to reattach cables to the solar panels while working partly inside the airless, darkened Spektr module, damaged when Mir collided with its resupply ship on June 25. The space station has run on reduced power since then, with some areas and experiments shut down to conserve energy.

"On August 20 when we plug in all the energy systems the whole complex will start its work almost as it was before," Solovyov told a news conference on Monday. "Nothing terrible or tragic has happened."
But the repairs will be risky. Space officials say the Spektr may contain dangerous floating chemicals or debris, and a puncture in a space suit could mean a swift death.

U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, the third member of the crew, will wait in the Soyuz escape vehicle during the repair. He is due to leave Mir in late September, to be replaced by David Wolf, who is currently training outside Moscow.

As Solovyov put forward a confident outlook the current Mir crew continued to try to restore the Elektron oxygen generating equipment, which has not worked for several days, perhaps because of air trapped in one of its pumps, NASA reported.
"They're still working on the Elektron," NASA spokeswoman Kathleen Maliga said on Monday evening from Mission Control outside Moscow. "They spent most of the day working on that."
The Mir, made up of different modules, has a back-up oxygen system, but it is in the Kvant-2 module which has been shut off to preserve energy.
The crew was planning to release some oxygen from canisters on board, and engineers at Mission Control were studying the matter, Maliga said.
Asked if the oxygen situation was a problem, Maliga said: "Not yet...Eventually you obviously need it to work."

The two Russians due to leave the Mir later this month, commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin, have faced crisis after crisis since taking residence in orbit in February. Vinogradov, who will blast off into space for the first time on Tuesday, said such troubles were to be expected.
"We are like babies in space, we've just started to work there," he told reporters. "We are only learning to work though we've been there for 40 years already. But these are only our first steps."
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.
